reading.body:
CyrusOne's Houston campus is the largest data center in Texas that publishes its power draw, at 84 MW across two buildings.

That figure is 18 percent of the 475 MW that Texas facilities disclose in total, across 19 sites. The state has 133 mapped data centers, so the disclosed capacity covers a small minority of the built estate. The 84 MW is a floor on what exists in Texas, not a measure of it. The campus holds 347,000 square feet of technical space and a Green Globes certification, which speaks to building operations rather than to whether the site can carry AI training loads.

For AI specifically, the useful conversion is density. At 40 kW per rack, 84 MW is roughly 2,100 racks. At 10 kW per GPU, it is roughly 8,400 high-end accelerators if the whole campus were allocated to GPU compute. Those are arithmetic on the published number, not a statement about how the site is actually used, and the data does not say what share of the load serves AI rather than conventional cloud or enterprise workloads.

What the data cannot answer is the question that matters most for scaling. It does not include the interconnection status, the contracted grid capacity, or any announced expansion, which the suitability score lists as a missing input. Texas grid constraint is the binding issue for any campus of this size, and nothing here describes how this one is served or how much more power it could draw. The ranking is real, but it ranks disclosure, not supply.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
